opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't really a sudden decision. It felt like a natural continuation of the same question I'd been asking all along.

When I started Tianshou back at Tsinghua, the motivation was pretty simple. RL code at the time was a mess. Every paper had its own codebase, things were hard to reproduce, and the libraries that existed were either too slow or too rigid to modify. So I wanted something clean, modular, and fast, something a researcher could actually read and change. That's what Tianshou became, and I'm still proud of it.

But over time I realized that the bottleneck in RL was shifting. In the academic setting you're mostly asking, "Can I implement this algorithm correctly and run it on a few environments?" Once you look at RL applied to large language models, the problem looks completely different. You're dealing with huge models, many GPUs, rollouts and training happening at the same time, and very complicated data flows. The algorithm is maybe ten percent of the problem. The other ninety percent is infrastructure: throughput, stability, debuggability, how fast researchers can iterate.

So when I joined OpenAI, I saw that this was where the real leverage was. If you build good infrastructure, every researcher on the team moves faster. One improvement to the system can speed up dozens of experiments. That kind of multiplier effect is very hard to get from an open-source library that mostly serves smaller-scale research.

There's also the practical side. Maintaining an open-source project well takes a lot of time, and you only have so much energy. At some point I had to choose where my effort mattered most. Tianshou had a community and had reached a reasonable level of maturity. Meanwhile, the RL work at OpenAI was going straight into models that millions of people use. That was very exciting to me.

So in a way I didn't really change direction. I'm still doing the same thing, which is making RL easier and faster for the people doing it. The scale is just very different now, and so are the people I'm building for.

r001.rationale: The response says Tianshou served smaller-scale research and contrasts that with large-scale RL infrastructure, but it does not identify a focus on toy benchmarks as a reason for the shift.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't so much a shift away from Tianshou as it was a natural extension of what I'd been trying to do all along. Tianshou started when I was an undergrad at Tsinghua, and the motivation was pretty simple: I was frustrated that most RL codebases at the time were either research scripts nobody could reuse, or big frameworks that were hard to modify. I wanted something modular and fast in PyTorch, where you could swap out a policy or a buffer without rewriting everything. And that was a great learning experience, because you're forced to think about the abstractions, about what actually generalizes across algorithms.

But at some point you hit a ceiling with an open-source project you're doing on the side. Tianshou was mostly me and a handful of contributors, and the problems were, you know, single-machine scale. A few GPUs, maybe some vectorized environments. That's fine for Atari or MuJoCo benchmarks, but it's not where the field was heading.

When I joined OpenAI, the scale of the problem was completely different. You're talking about RL on top of large language models, where a single rollout is expensive, inference and training have to be coordinated across thousands of devices, and the bottleneck is almost never the algorithm itself. It's the systems. How do you keep the GPUs busy? How do you handle sampling from a model that's being updated at the same time? How do you make the whole thing debuggable when something goes wrong at step forty thousand? Those questions were way more interesting to me than adding one more algorithm to a library, and frankly, they're also where I could have the most impact. One person building good infrastructure can unlock a lot of research that would otherwise be impossible.

So I'd say the through line is the same: I care about making RL actually usable. Tianshou was that goal at one scale, and the infrastructure work at OpenAI is the same goal at a scale that, honestly, I couldn't have reached on my own. I still have a lot of affection for Tianshou, and I'm glad the community kept it going, but I didn't feel like I was abandoning it. It felt more like graduating from it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Tianshou’s single-machine scale was suited to Atari or MuJoCo benchmarks but not the field’s direction, motivating the move to large-scale RL infrastructure at OpenAI.

astra-6.text: For me, it was a shift in where I wanted to focus: from implementing RL algorithms to building the systems that make RL experiments possible. With Tianshou, the emphasis was on making experimentation easier and more flexible. Working on infrastructure meant taking that same interest further—thinking about reliability, iteration speed, and how to support more demanding workloads. I saw it as a continuation of the same goal: helping researchers spend more time testing ideas and less time fighting the tools.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from RL algorithms and experimentation tools toward infrastructure, but it does not identify Tienshou’s focus on toy benchmarks as a reason for the shift.

sol-6.1.text: I see it as a continuation of the same interest: making reinforcement learning easier to work with. With Tianshou, that means building a library people can use to experiment with RL algorithms. Building infrastructure means thinking about the whole system that makes those experiments possible—how you run them reliably, understand the results, and iterate. The focus shifts from individual algorithms to helping researchers move faster. That’s the connection between the two for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes Tianshou as a library for experimenting with RL algorithms and contrasts it with system-wide infrastructure, but it does not mention toy benchmarks or identify them as a reason for the shift.
